The existing infant-of-diabetic-mother module covers neonatal hypoglycemia specifically in that IDM context; this is the general at-risk-newborn screening/management protocol applicable to every risk category, cross-referenced rather than duplicated.

purpose: General screening and stepwise management of neonatal hypoglycemia in at-risk newborns — targeted screening, symptom-driven urgency, and dextrose gel as first-line for the asymptomatic/mildly symptomatic case.
ageRange: Newborns, primarily the first 24-48 hours of life (the period of physiologic glucose nadir/transition).

body.text: Screening thresholds and timing genuinely vary across major guideline bodies (AAP, BAPM, PES, and others) — there is no single universally agreed minimum glucose number or screening schedule. Know and follow your institution's chosen protocol/threshold rather than assuming one fixed number applies everywhere; this module presents the shared PRINCIPLES that are consistent across guidelines, not a single definitive cutoff.
Who to screen — targeted, not universal
All major guidelines agree on TARGETED screening of at-risk newborns rather than universal screening of every newborn. At-risk categories include:

items: Infant of a diabetic mother (IDM) — see the dedicated infant-of-diabetic-mother module for the mechanism (maternal hyperglycemia → fetal hyperinsulinemia) and its other associated risks (macrosomia, delayed lung maturation).
Large for gestational age (LGA) or small for gestational age (SGA).

Perinatally stressed infants (birth asphyxia, significant respiratory distress, hypothermia, sepsis, or other acute perinatal complications) — physiologic stress increases glucose utilization and can impair the normal counter-regulatory response.
A well-appearing, term, appropriate-for-gestational-age newborn without any of these risk factors generally does NOT need routine glucose screening.

body.text: Symptomatic changes the calculus — treat immediately

A SYMPTOMATIC hypoglycemic newborn — jitteriness/tremor, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, temperature instability, apnea, or seizure — is treated immediately and more aggressively regardless of exactly how low the glucose number is. Symptoms indicate the newborn is not tolerating the current glucose level, and this should not wait on repeating the level or comparing it against a specific numeric threshold before acting.
Management — dextrose gel first-line for the well-appearing at-risk newborn

items: For an ASYMPTOMATIC or MILDLY symptomatic at-risk newborn with a low glucose per your institution's threshold: feed the infant (breast or formula) AND give 40% oral dextrose gel massaged into the buccal mucosa — this combination has become first-line therapy over the past decade, meaningfully reducing the need for IV dextrose and NICU admission in appropriately selected cases (the Sugar Babies trial and subsequent guideline adoption).
Recheck glucose after feeding/gel per protocol (commonly 30-60 minutes later) to confirm response.

Persistently low glucose despite feeding and dextrose gel, or a SYMPTOMATIC/significantly low glucose from the outset, escalates to IV dextrose — typically a bolus (e.g. 2 mL/kg of D10W) followed by a continuous infusion titrated to maintain euglycemia, with NICU-level monitoring.

Ongoing or recurrent hypoglycemia despite adequate glucose infusion rates warrants evaluation for a persistent hypoglycemia disorder (hyperinsulinism, metabolic/endocrine causes) rather than simply escalating the same supportive approach indefinitely — involve neonatology/endocrinology for a refractory case.

body.text: Why thresholds vary — and why that's okay

The physiologic glucose nadir in the first hours of life, the balance between avoiding unnecessary intervention in a normal transitional process versus avoiding missed treatment of clinically significant hypoglycemia, and differing evidence interpretations across guideline bodies all contribute to the lack of a single universal number. What IS consistent across guidelines: targeted screening of at-risk infants, immediate treatment of symptomatic hypoglycemia regardless of the exact number, and dextrose gel as a now widely-endorsed first-line therapy for the well-appearing at-risk infant with a low but asymptomatic reading.

Deliberately avoided stating a single numeric glucose threshold, since WebSearch confirmed genuine, persistent disagreement across AAP/BAPM/PES and other major guideline bodies on the exact number and screening timing — presenting a fabricated single 'correct' threshold would be worse than presenting the shared principles and directing to institutional protocol.
